title: Why the sky is blue
text: Sunlight sets out {{1}} the Sun and takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth, yet the journey does not end there. White light is made {{2}} of every colour, and when it strikes air molecules the shortest wavelengths are scattered in all directions, {{3}} is why a cloudless sky appears blue rather than black. At sunset the geometry reverses: light must cross far more air, most of the blue is filtered {{4}} long before it reaches the ground, and orange and red come to dominate the horizon. Fine volcanic dust intensifies the effect, a pattern that has repeated {{5}} after every great eruption in recorded history. Very {{6}} of the light that survives such a journey is blue, which helps to explain the warm palettes favoured by painters in dusty cities. Astronauts see none of this display: from orbit, they look down at {{7}} thin bright rim of the atmosphere and, beyond it, the black of space, for {{8}} is no air there to paint a sky.

gaps.explanation: 'Sets out from' — from marks the starting point of the journey.
'Made up of' is the fixed three-part phrase for composition.
A sentential relative after the comma; 'that' is impossible here.
'Filter out' — the particle completes the phrasal verb meaning 'remove'.
The pattern is both subject and object: it has repeated itself.
'Very little' for an uncountable quantity; 'few' cannot go before 'of the light'.

gaps.hint: article: look down at ___ thin bright rim
gaps.explanation: The atmosphere is already known from context, so the definite article is required.

gaps.hint: pronoun: for __ is no air there
gaps.explanation: The dummy subject 'there' introduces the existential clause 'there is no air'.
